anonymous redactorial voice of this passage

the Sages of the tzrif mishnah quoted at 7b.17 (וחכמים מכשירין)
Mar Keshisha brei deRav Chisda, addressing Rav Ashi (8a.6)
the judges of Caesarea -- the ואמרי לה naming of the same speakers
the ואמרי לה tradition at 8a.10 naming the speakers the judges of Caesarea

props.gloss_en: the mishnah: a sukkah whose sunlight exceeds its shade is invalid
the baraita's first view: 'its sunlight' means sunlight through the sekhakh, not through the walls
R' Yoshiya: sunlight through the walls counts too
Abaye: R' Yoshiya's reason is the verse 'and you shall screen (vesakota) the ark with the curtain' -- the curtain is a partition, and the Torah calls it sekhakh
Abaye's criterion: hence we require a partition to be like sekhakh
and the Rabbis? that verse [teaches] that one bends [the curtain] a little, so that it looks like sekhakh
Abaye: Rabbi holds a sukkah must be a fixed dwelling
Abaye: R' Yoshiya holds the same
Abaye: R' Yehuda holds the same
Abaye: R' Shimon holds the same
Abaye: Rabban Gamliel holds the same
Abaye: Beit Shammai hold the same
Abaye: R' Eliezer holds the same
Abaye: Acherim hold the same
Rabbi: any sukkah without four amot by four amot is invalid (cited again at 7b.20)
the mishnah: a sukkah higher than twenty amot is invalid (same content as sukkah_2a_gubhah_sukkah's p_mishnah_psul)
R' Yehuda validates it
the baraita's first view: two walls in the standard sense and a third even of a tefach
R' Shimon: three walls in the standard sense and a fourth even of a tefach
one who makes his sukkah atop a wagon or atop a ship: Rabban Gamliel invalidates
and R' Akiva validates
one whose head and most of his body were in the sukkah and his table inside the house: Beit Shammai invalidate
and Beit Hillel validate
one who makes his sukkah like a tzrif (a sloping hut), or leans it against a wall: R' Eliezer invalidates
R' Eliezer's reason: because it has no roof
and the Sages validate
Acherim: a sukkah made like a dovecote is invalid
Acherim's reason: because it has no corners
R' Yochanan: a furnace-shaped (round) sukkah is valid if its circumference has room for twenty-four people to sit, otherwise invalid
like whom? like Rabbi, who requires four amot by four
the reckoning's premise: a man sits in an amah (reasserted by Rav Asi at 8a.8: לעולם גברא באמתא יתיב)
the first answer to the third reckoning: [R' Yochanan] was not precise (24 against 17 less a fifth)
Mar Keshisha to Rav Ashi: do you suppose a man sits in an amah? three men sit in two amot
on that premise twenty-four men make sixteen, and we need seventeen less a fifth -- he was not precise (i.e. imprecise toward leniency)
Rav Asi to Rav Ashi: a man does sit in an amah, and R' Yochanan does not count the place of the men themselves
on that reading it comes to eighteen, where seventeen less a fifth suffices -- that is where he was not precise, and imprecise toward stringency
the Rabbis of Caesarea: a circle inside a square [falls short of it by] a quarter; a square inside a circle [falls short by] a half -- so twenty-four is the circle around a sixteen-amah square

answered_by.gloss_en: הני מילי בעיגול דנפיק מגו ריבועא, אבל ריבועא דנפיק מגו עיגולא -- בעינן טפי, משום מורשא דקרנתא: that is a circle inside a square; a square inside a circle needs more, for the projecting corners

objections.gloss_en: מכדי כל אמתא בריבועא אמתא ותרי חומשי באלכסונא -- בשיבסר נכי חומשא סגיא? the diagonal of an amah is 1 2/5, so seventeen less a fifth should suffice.
